paragraphs.heading: One version hides another
paragraphs.text: A gene can come in different versions, called alleles. A cell can carry one allele of a gene on one copy of a chromosome and a different allele on the other copy. Dominance is when one of those alleles masks or overrides the effect of the other. The allele that wins out is called dominant, and the one that is hidden is called recessive.

paragraphs.heading: Round and wrinkled peas
paragraphs.text: An often-cited example is the shape of pea seeds. A pea plant's seeds can be round, linked to the allele R, or wrinkled, linked to the allele r. That gives three possible pairings, or genotypes: RR, Rr and rr. RR plants and rr plants carry two matching alleles, and they make round and wrinkled peas respectively. Rr plants carry one of each, yet their peas are round, because R masks r.

paragraphs.heading: Mendel and the 3:1 ratio
paragraphs.text: Gregor Mendel, often called the father of genetics, put forward the idea of dominance in the 1860s, though it only became widely known in the early twentieth century. Working with garden peas, he found that lines bred on their own kept the same form of a trait, such as tall or short plants, generation after generation. He then crossed lines with different forms. Each hybrid offspring showed just one of the parents' traits. When he crossed those hybrids with each other, both original traits came back, in a ratio of three to one.

paragraphs.heading: Why three to one
paragraphs.text: Mendel reasoned that in the first cross one parent was AA and the other aa, and each passed one allele to the offspring. So the hybrids all carried one A and one a, and A masked a. Crossing two such hybrids yields three kinds of offspring, AA, Aa and aa, in the proportions 1:2:1. The first two kinds both look like A, which yields the 3:1 ratio of appearances. Mendel also started the habit, still used today, of writing dominant alleles in capital letters and recessive ones in lower case.

paragraphs.heading: Not all-or-nothing
paragraphs.text: Dominance is not always complete. In incomplete dominance, an individual with two different alleles looks different from both pure types, often somewhere in between. Snapdragons show this: crossing a red-flowered plant with a white-flowered one gives pink flowers. In co-dominance, by contrast, both alleles show their own traits at once.

paragraphs.heading: A relationship, not a property
paragraphs.text: Being dominant is not a fixed quality of an allele. It only describes how two alleles of the same gene behave together. A single allele can mask a second allele, be masked by a third, and show co-dominance alongside a fourth. It may also be dominant for one trait but not for others. Dominance should not be confused with epistasis, where an allele of one gene masks the effect of a different gene.
